questions.q: In the Prisoner's Dilemma each player chooses Cooperate or Defect, with payoffs (higher is better): if both Cooperate each gets $3$; if both Defect each gets $1$; if one Defects while the other Cooperates the defector gets $5$ and the cooperator gets $0$. Which statement is correct?
choices: Defect strictly dominates Cooperate for each player, so $(D,D)$ is the unique Nash equilibrium even though $(C,C)$ Pareto-dominates it
Cooperate strictly dominates Defect, so $(C,C)$ is the unique equilibrium
Neither strategy dominates the other, so there is no pure equilibrium
$(C,C)$ is the unique Nash equilibrium because it maximizes total payoff
questions.explain: Hold the opponent fixed. If they Cooperate, Defecting gives $5 > 3$; if they Defect, Defecting gives $1 > 0$. So Defect beats Cooperate against every opponent action — it strictly dominates. Both players reason this way, landing on $(D,D)$ with payoff $1$ each, even though $(C,C)$ gives $3$ each. The conflict between individual incentives and the Pareto-superior outcome is the whole point of the dilemma.

questions.q: A pure strategy $s_i$ of player $i$ is strictly dominated when:
choices: there is another strategy $s_i'$ giving player $i$ strictly higher payoff for every strategy profile of the opponents
$s_i$ gives a lower payoff than $s_i'$ for at least one opponent profile
$s_i$ is never a best response to any single opponent strategy
$s_i$ gives player $i$ the lowest payoff in the entire matrix
questions.explain: Strict dominance requires that the dominating strategy $s_i'$ beat $s_i$ against every opponent profile, simultaneously. (Weak dominance only asks for $\ge$ everywhere with strict somewhere.) A strictly dominated strategy is never played in any Nash equilibrium, which is why iterated elimination of strictly dominated strategies is a sound first step.

questions.q: Which data are part of the specification of a finite game in normal (strategic) form?
choices: A finite set of players
For each player, a finite set of pure strategies
For each player, a payoff function on the profiles of all players' strategies
A fixed order in which players move
questions.explain: Normal form is exactly (players, strategy sets, payoff functions). It is simultaneous-move by construction — there is no notion of move order; that timing structure belongs to the extensive (game-tree) form, not the normal form.

questions.q: A strategy profile $s^* = (s_1^*, \dots, s_n^*)$ is a Nash equilibrium when:
choices: no player can strictly increase their own payoff by unilaterally changing strategy while the others hold fixed
every player is using a strictly dominant strategy
the sum of all players' payoffs is maximized
all players receive equal payoffs
questions.explain: Nash equilibrium is a mutual best-response condition: each $s_i^*$ is a best response to $s_{-i}^*$, so no unilateral deviation helps. It need not maximize total welfare (the Prisoner's Dilemma equilibrium does not), need not be symmetric, and need not involve dominant strategies.

questions.q: Nash's existence theorem guarantees that every finite game has at least one Nash equilibrium. In what sense, and via what tool?
choices: In mixed strategies, proved by applying Kakutani's fixed-point theorem to the best-response correspondence
In pure strategies, proved by backward induction
In mixed strategies, proved by the simplex method
Only for zero-sum games, proved by LP duality
questions.explain: Pure equilibria can fail to exist (matching pennies has none). Nash's theorem secures a mixed-strategy equilibrium for every finite game. The proof puts the best-response correspondence on the compact convex product of strategy simplices and applies Kakutani's fixed-point theorem; a fixed point is precisely a profile where everyone best-responds to everyone, i.e. a Nash equilibrium.

questions.q: Consider the $2\times2$ coordination game where players pick A or B: payoffs are $(2,2)$ at $(A,A)$, $(1,1)$ at $(B,B)$, and $(0,0)$ at the two mismatched cells. Which are the pure Nash equilibria?
choices: $(A,A)$ and $(B,B)$
$(A,A)$ only
$(A,B)$ and $(B,A)$
There are no pure equilibria
questions.explain: At $(A,A)$ neither player gains by switching to B (payoff drops $2 \to 0$); same at $(B,B)$ ($1 \to 0$). The mismatched cells are not equilibria — either player can move to a matching cell and raise their payoff from $0$. So both $(A,A)$ and $(B,B)$ are pure Nash equilibria (there is also a mixed one); coordination games typically have multiple equilibria.

questions.q: Von Neumann's minimax theorem for a two-player zero-sum game with payoff matrix $A$ (row player maximizes $x^\top A y$, column player minimizes) states that:
choices: $\max_x \min_y x^\top A y = \min_y \max_x x^\top A y$, the common value being the value $v$ of the game
$\max_x \min_y x^\top A y < \min_y \max_x x^\top A y$ in general
the game always has a pure-strategy saddle point
the value of the game is the average of all matrix entries
questions.explain: The max-min (what the row player can guarantee) always lower-bounds the min-max (what the column player can hold them to). Minimax asserts equality once mixed strategies are allowed: $\max_x\min_y x^\top A y = \min_y\max_x x^\top A y = v$. A pure saddle point exists only when the game has one; mixing is what closes the gap in general.

questions.q: Why is the minimax theorem said to be equivalent to LP duality?
choices: The row player's optimal mixed strategy solves a linear program whose dual is solved by the column player's optimal strategy, and strong duality forces the two optimal values to coincide at $v$
Because every zero-sum game is itself a linear program with no constraints
Because the simplex method is the only way to find a Nash equilibrium
Because LP duality only applies to symmetric games
questions.explain: Maximizing the value the row player can guarantee is an LP (maximize $v$ subject to $x^\top A \ge v\mathbf{1}$, $x$ a distribution). Its dual is exactly the column player's value-minimization LP. Strong duality says the optimal primal and dual objectives are equal — which is precisely $\max_x\min_y = \min_y\max_x = v$. So minimax and LP strong duality are two faces of one theorem.

questions.q: Matching pennies as a zero-sum game has payoff matrix $A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ (row player's payoff). What is the value $v$ of the game?
questions.explain: By symmetry each player mixes $(\tfrac12,\tfrac12)$. Then $x^\top A y = \tfrac14(1-1-1+1) = 0$, and neither player can do better, so the value is $v = 0$. There is no pure saddle point — the equality $\max_x\min_y = \min_y\max_x = 0$ holds only because mixed strategies are allowed.

questions.q: The indifference principle for a mixed Nash equilibrium says that:
choices: each player makes the other indifferent among all pure strategies in the support of that other player's mix
each player is indifferent among all of their own pure strategies, used or not
both players must receive the same expected payoff
a player only randomizes over strategies that strictly dominate the rest
questions.explain: If a player randomizes over several pure strategies in equilibrium, every one of those must yield the same expected payoff against the opponent's mix — otherwise the player would shift all weight to the best one. So in a mixed equilibrium, each player chooses their own probabilities to make the opponent exactly indifferent over the opponent's support. This is the equation you solve to find the mix.

questions.q: In matching pennies the row player wins $+1$ on a match and loses $1$ on a mismatch (column player opposite). Let the column player play Heads with probability $q$. For the row player to be indifferent between Heads and Tails, what value must $q$ take?
questions.explain: Row's payoff to Heads is $q(1) + (1-q)(-1) = 2q - 1$; to Tails it is $q(-1) + (1-q)(1) = 1 - 2q$. Indifference $2q-1 = 1-2q$ gives $q = \tfrac12$. By symmetry the row player also mixes $\tfrac12$/$\tfrac12$, so the unique (mixed) Nash equilibrium is $\big((\tfrac12,\tfrac12),(\tfrac12,\tfrac12)\big)$.

questions.q: Matching pennies has no pure-strategy Nash equilibrium. Why does an equilibrium still exist?
choices: Nash's theorem guarantees a mixed equilibrium for every finite game; here it is each player mixing $\tfrac12$/$\tfrac12$
Because one player has a strictly dominant strategy
Because the game is symmetric, the diagonal cells are equilibria
It does not — matching pennies is a counterexample to Nash's theorem
questions.explain: In every pure cell of matching pennies one player wants to switch (the loser flips to win), so no pure equilibrium exists. But Nash's theorem promises a mixed equilibrium, and the indifference computation gives it: both players randomize uniformly, making each indifferent and removing any profitable deviation.

questions.q: In a transferable-utility cooperative game with characteristic function $v$, an allocation $x = (x_1,\dots,x_n)$ is in the core when:
choices: $\sum_i x_i = v(N)$ (efficiency) and $\sum_{i\in S} x_i \ge v(S)$ for every coalition $S$ (no coalition can do better alone)
$x_i = v(\{i\})$ for every player
every player receives the same amount $v(N)/n$
$x_i$ equals player $i$'s Shapley value
questions.explain: The core is the set of efficient allocations of the grand coalition's worth $v(N)$ that are coalitionally stable: no subset $S$ could secure more than $\sum_{i\in S}x_i$ by breaking away, i.e. $\sum_{i\in S}x_i \ge v(S)$ for all $S$. The core can be large, a single point, or empty; the Shapley value need not lie in it.

questions.q: Three players form a $1$-unit-value game: $v(S) = 1$ for any coalition $S$ containing player $1$ and at least one other player, $v(N) = 1$, and $v(S) = 0$ for all coalitions of size $\le 1$ and for $\{2,3\}$. Player $1$ is essential to every productive coalition. What is the Shapley value $\varphi_1$ of player $1$?
questions.explain: Average player $1$'s marginal contribution over all $3! = 6$ orderings. Player $1$ contributes $1$ unless they arrive first (no coalition yet, contributes $0$): they arrive first in $2$ of the $6$ orderings. So $\varphi_1 = \tfrac{1}{6}(0+0+1+1+1+1) = \tfrac{4}{6} = \tfrac{2}{3} \approx 0.667$. Players $2$ and $3$ split the remaining $\tfrac13$ equally, $\varphi_2 = \varphi_3 = \tfrac16$.

questions.q: The Shapley value is the unique allocation rule satisfying which axioms?
choices: Efficiency: the payoffs sum to $v(N)$
Symmetry: interchangeable players get equal shares
Dummy (null) player: a player contributing nothing to any coalition gets $0$
Additivity: the value of a sum of two games is the sum of the values
questions.explain: Shapley's theorem: there is exactly one value satisfying efficiency, symmetry, the dummy axiom, and additivity, and it is the average marginal contribution $\varphi_i = \frac{1}{n!}\sum_{\text{orderings}} [v(\text{predecessors}\cup\{i\}) - v(\text{predecessors})]$. All four axioms are needed for uniqueness.

questions.q: In a sealed-bid second-price (Vickrey) auction for a single item, the highest bidder wins and pays the second-highest bid. Why is bidding your true valuation a dominant strategy?
choices: Your bid only decides whether you win, never what you pay (that is set by others), so bidding truthfully wins exactly the profitable auctions and never causes a loss
Because the seller forces all bidders to bid their valuation
Because the second-highest bid always equals your valuation
Because shading your bid downward increases the price you pay
questions.explain: Your own bid in a second-price auction never sets your price — the runner-up's bid does. Bidding above your value can only make you win a too-expensive auction (paying more than it is worth); bidding below can only make you lose an auction you would have profited from. Bidding exactly your value $v_i$ is weakly dominant: you win iff the price is below $v_i$, which is exactly when winning is profitable. The single-item Vickrey auction is the simplest VCG mechanism.

questions.q: How does a first-price auction (winner pays their own bid) differ strategically from a second-price auction?
choices: In a first-price auction bidders shade their bids below their valuations to leave room for surplus, so truthful bidding is not a dominant strategy
In a first-price auction truthful bidding is still dominant
A first-price auction always raises more revenue with certainty
The two auctions always produce identical bids
questions.explain: In a first-price auction your bid is your price, so bidding your true value $v_i$ yields zero surplus when you win. Rational bidders shade down, and the optimal shade depends on beliefs about rivals — so truthtelling is not dominant and equilibrium bidding requires a Bayesian model. The second-price auction removes this coupling, which is exactly why truthful bidding becomes dominant there.

questions.q: Suppose three bidders have valuations $\$10$, $\$7$, $\$4$ for an item and all bid truthfully in a second-price auction. Who wins and what do they pay?
choices: The $\$10$ bidder wins and pays $\$7$
The $\$10$ bidder wins and pays $\$10$
The $\$7$ bidder wins and pays $\$4$
The $\$10$ bidder wins and pays $\$4$
questions.explain: Highest bidder wins (the $\$10$ valuation) and pays the second-highest bid, $\$7$. Their surplus is $\$10 - \$7 = \$3 > 0$, confirming truthful bidding was safe. The mechanism allocates the item efficiently (to the highest-value bidder) while charging the externality the winner imposes — the runner-up's forgone value.
